The problem with Linux adoption is that even after you explain the ABSOLUTELY SUPERNATURAL effort that goes into Wine, Crossover, the kernel, the wide variety of GUIs, the vast and amazing amount of text manipulation, the fact that all of computer science from 1950-ish onward has a native and free compiler when just a few years ago a millionth of it would cost 10 grand, the carefully orchestrated web of programmers working or volunteering for every level from assembly systems programming all the way up to high level natural language stuff... people are still like "but muh gaymes". It's seriously fucking ludicrous.

Not if you don't know how to configure it. It's too easy to take a lot of this knowledge for granted; what is easy for a highly technical person makes someone who's isn't and never will be break down in tears out of frustration, assuming they have the time or drive to try to learn it in the first place.

Frankly most of what you mention is interesting to computer science professionals first and foremost, if not exclusively. The text processing tools aren't of much use to most people, even if they're easy for someone used to a CLI to work with, and for all the power it may offer I'll bet you that you're not going to sell raw TeX to most people, either, even if you push Word compatibility aside. Developer tools aren't much, if any, better (in fact, they're arguably worse). And a lot of the programmer network you cite is of extremely variable help to these people. I've heard enough stories about how someone got their head bitten off for asking a simple question, resulting in someone who pretty much gave up on Linux before they even really started.

These computer science advances are important for computer scientists, and how one builds programs. But it's not an advance in how end users use computers. It's like knowing about charms and quarks and how they've had an impact in subatomic physics - some random person off the street won't have a lot, if any, knowledge of it, let alone how to put any of it to use. "Muh games" may be the only reason they bother with something other than an iPhone in the first place outside of work, and they simply don't have the time or inclination to deal with desktop headaches otherwise. There are good, user-friendly ways of working with a Unix type system. Mac OS X and Android are two prime ones. However, conventional Linux generally isn't there yet.

There are a lot of problems, and a lot of rough edges, and some of those rough edges go pretty deep down the rabbit hole. Case in point - trying to install arbitrary software that isn't in the package manager repository. Unless you go and luck out, and there's actually a package put out by someone that's actually compatible with your distribution (it is usually invariably for the opposite of what you're using, deb vs rpm, or it's the wrong specific distro or distro version, or it was compiled against a library you don't have and don't know where to get, and so forth), you're gonna have problems. To solve that takes knowledge of how to compile (contrary to popular belief, 'make ; make install' is far from foolproof and if that doesn't work you're pretty boned, especially if you have to manually edit source code, and I have had to do so), or knowledge of the directory structure, or hope that the custom install/uninstall program that unceremoniously drops binaries into /usr/local/bin works and doesn't need a specific version of some library you've never heard of... it's seriously a mess, and although it's gotten somewhat better since the 90's on that count, there are still a lot of pitfalls. And even though it tends to work for some people, doesn't mean it works for everyone. Yes, there are grandmas that use Ubuntu. But they use a relatively narrowly-defined cross section of applications that are well defined that come with the distro as front-line default programs which are well-maintained for automatic updates. Usually just the web browser, word processor and maybe e-mail client or drawing program. The easy to use Linux distributions start showing problems if you're in the gulf between "extremely extremely casual user" and "server administrator who can write shell script code on the fly." Insurmountable problems? Not at all. But enough to prevent people from taking it up, or interfering? Yes. Myself, I've been working with Linux since the mid-90s and I have had very little luck with Wine, for instance. Crossover worked pretty well when I desperately needed Word on my Linux machine at one point, but plain Wine, never worked very well at all. I find it more useful to just virtualize when I need cross-platform software (which is a tremendous advance in itself, but that's neither here nor there). Even if the game is compatible with Wine, you have to worry about what patch level you're on, which may mean weeks or months of outages if you're playing on an MMO. And a response of "you want to see it done, do it yourself" is going to result in a new Windows installation (and as well all know, every time Windows is installed afresh, Cthulhu gets his wings... or something).

These problems are all too often glossed over or used to dismiss Linux. These are both very poor attitudes to have. I have had at least one idiot on here claim I hate Linux because I wasn't impressed that some YouTube video showed some cool stuff you could do with Linux without addressing problems someone might actually have on a daily basis. Well, if people want to reach normal desktop users, these issues are going to have to be addressed, and addressed in a manner that does not involve telling them to go configure it. They're going to stare at the text file, shake their heads, realize they don't want to spend months learning to configure it, and go install Windows. The fact that some people manage to do really awesome things with Linux is of only limited help, as well - I've seen, say, Enlightenment desktops that have had hours upon hours of hand-tweaking configuration to make an awesome, highly-automated, stylish desktop. These have been around since the late 90s. These also don't go into how much raw work it took to customize it. Things aren't nearly as bad now as they were then, but it still illustrates the point, painful though it may be to face.

It is my hope that the day of desktop Linux will come. An alternative to Windows is desperately needed, and although Linux is in the position to offer that, it could do much better. The day of the Linux desktop isn't today, and trying to pretend that this isn't the case or that it's all the fault of the users is not going to speed it along. If anything, it will only push it that much closer to never coming to fruition in the first place.
